newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Clashes erupt in South Korea after arrests.
newsitem.headline: Clashes erupt in South Korea after arrests.

text.p: Riot police fired volleys of teargas on Thursday to block thousands of workers from marching on Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral where seven labour leaders are sheltering from arrest.
Clashes erupted after authorities seized three more union leaders in a crackdown on strikes sparked by the passage of a controversial labour law.
Witnesses said the workers repeatedly surged towards the cathedral but were repelled by stinging teargas.

Some 10,000 workers converged on a warren of narrow shopping alleys around the cathedral in central Seoul from rallies around the capital. Riot police have thrown a tight security cordon around the red-brick church.
Squads of officers carrying clubs and shields were confronting the vast crowds, witnesses said.
Police swooped during the night on the three shipyard unionists after authorities warned that three weeks of industrial unrest was being fanned by North Korea to topple the government.

In response, the president of the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, Kwon Young-kil, who is camped out in the cathedral along with six deputies, warned that strikes could be prolonged for another two months. Although the chairman of the ruling party extended an olive branch to strikers, arrest orders remained in force for a total of 16 unionists.
A call for a general strike on Tuesday and Wednesday went largely unheeded, but 15,000 workers fought pitched battles with riot police in Seoul on the second day.

On Thursday, industrial action was still sputtering at several major car plants, hospitals, state broadcasters and 10 regional newspapers. But shipyards were working normally and transport services were running smoothly.
The outlawed confederation said 260,000 of its half a million members had walked out, but the labour ministry put the number at 80,000 out of a total workforce of 12 million.
Officials said strikes had cost 2.4 trillion won ($2.8 billion) in lost production and $440 million in lost exports.

The issue that sparked the unrest -- passage of a labour law that allows companies to lay off workers and replace strikers -- remained explosive, and any attempt to arrest the Myongdong unionists could ignite fresh passions.
Four world labour leaders left the country after being threatened with deporation by authorities angry at what they viewed as foreign meddling in the strikes.
A British member of the team was due to report to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) on the new law and on threats against union leaders.

The OECD, which South Korea joined last December, has expressed concern about worker rights in South Korea under the law that maintains a monoploy on union representation by the officially sanctioned Federation of Korean Trade Unions.
The Paris-based club of rich nations has scheduled a meeting for January 22 to review the legislation.
The three arrested union leaders from Halla Heavy Industries were charged with obstructing business and beating workers who refused to down tools.
Another Halla Heavy union leader was arrested on Tuesday night on similar charges.
"The confederation could prolong the current strikes for more than two months," Kwon told reporters.
The law was rammed through parliament on December 26 by the ruling New Korea Party in the absence of opposition deputies.
On Thursday, New Korea Party Chairman Lee Hong-koo expressed "humble regret" for the way the legislation was adopted but ruled out any revisions.

"I would like to use this occasion to make known again my willingness to resolve all problems through dialogue and compromise," Lee told a news conference. He promised steps to allay worker fears that the law could lead to layoffs.
